[L184] Electric fields can thread a classical Einstein-Rosen bridge. Maldacena and Susskind have recently
[L185] suggested that in a theory of dynamical gravity the entanglement of ordinary perturbative quanta
[L186] should be viewed as creating a quantum version of an Einstein-Rosen bridge between the particles,
[L187] or a “quantum wormhole.” We demonstrate within low-energy effective field theory that there is
[L188] a precise sense in which electric fields can also thread such quantum wormholes. We define a non￾perturbative “wormhole susceptibility” that measures the ease of passing an electric field through
[L189] any sort of wormhole. The susceptibility of a quantum wormhole is suppressed by powers of the
[L190] U(1) gauge coupling relative to that for a classical wormhole but can be made numerically equal
[L191] with a sufficiently large amount of entangled matter.
[L192] I. INTRODUCTION
[L193] The past decade has seen accumulating evidence of
[L194] a deep connection between classical spacetime geome￾try and the entanglement of quantum fields. In the
[L195] AdS/CFT context, there appears to be a precise holo￾graphic sense in which a classical geometry is “emergent”
[L196] from quantum entanglement in a dual field theory (see
[L197] e.g. [1–10]).
[L198] Recently, Maldacena and Susskind have made a
[L199] stronger statement: that the link between entangle￾ment and geometry exists even without any holographic
[L200] changes of duality frame [11]. They propose that any en￾tangled perturbative quantum matter in the bulk of a dy￾namical theory of gravity, such as an entangled Einstein￾Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) [12] pair of electrons, is connected
[L201] by a “quantum wormhole,” or some sort of Planckian,
[L202] highly fluctuating, version of the classical Einstein-Rosen
[L203] (ER) [13] bridge that connects the two sides of an eternal
[L204] black hole. Notably, while it clearly resonates well with
[L205] holographic ideas [14–29], this “ER = EPR” proposal
[L206] is more general in that it makes no reference to gauge￾gravity duality. The entangled quantum fields here exist
[L207] already in a theory of dynamical gravity rather than in
[L208] a holographically dual field theory.
[L209] It is not at all obvious that quantum wormholes so de￾fined – i.e. just ordinary entangled perturbative matter
[L210] – exhibit properties similar to those of classical worm￾holes. For example, if we have dynamical electromag￾netism, then the existence of a smooth geometry in the
[L211] throat of an Einstein-Rosen bridge means that there exist
[L212] states with a continuously tunable1
[L213] electric flux thread￾ing the wormhole, as shown in Figure 1.

[L450] 5.4 Modifying the theory
[L451] In order to resolve the paradox, there have been various suggestions to modify
[L452] the underlying physical/mathematical/logical theories by which we describe
[L453] the phenomena in question. Some of these endeavors are based on the observa￾tion that the violation of the Bell-type inequalities is deeply related to the non￾classical feature of quantum probability theory [35, 26, 24, 25]. More exactly,
[L454] it is rooted in the (non-distributive lattice) structure of the underlying event
[L455] algebra which essentially differs from the classical Boolean algebra. According
[L456] to some of these approaches, the fact in itself that the Bell-type inequalities are
[L457] violated has nothing to do with such physical questions as locality, causality or
[L458] the ontology of quantum phenomena. It is just a simple mathematical conse￾quence of quantum probability theory and/or quantum logic ([26], pp. 49–51;
[L459] 182–183).
[L460] According to another approach, it is quantum mechanics itself that has to
[L461] be modified. So called relational quantum mechanics [6, 33, 7] introduces a
[L462] new concept: the relative quantum state. It turns out that the relative quan￾tum state of the right particle changes if the left particle is measured and vice
[L463] versa. Therefore, it is argued, the two particles are not causally separated at a
[L464] quantum level.
[L465] Some papers, motivated by the problem of quantum gravity, suggest space￾time structures that are intrinsically based on quantum theory. These results
[L466] have remarkable interrelations with the EPR–Bell problem [38, 39, 37]. The EPR
[L467] events, which are spatially separated in classical space-time, turn out not to
[L468] be spatially separated in some other space-time structures based on quantum
[L469] mechanics.
[L470] 23Another branch of research attempts to develop, within the framework of
[L471] algebraic quantum field theory, an exact concept of “separation” of subsystems
[L472] [27, 31, 28, 29].
[L473] What is common to all these efforts is that they aim to improve the concep￾tual/theoretical means by which we describe and analyze the EPR–Bell prob￾lem. All these approaches, however, encounter the following difficulty: The
[L474] violation of the Bell-type inequalities is an experimental fact.

[L534] in section VI, I ponder the possibility of Einstein’s con￾cepts, ER bridges, and the EPR paradox being inter￾twined unexpectedly.
[L535] II. EPR: ELEMENTS OF REALITY
[L536] In early March 1935, Einstein, Rosen, and Podol￾sky submitted the manuscript of the EPR paper, "Can
[L537] Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be
[L538] Considered Complete?", to Physical Review, and it was
[L539] published on May 15, 1935 [1]
[L540] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky used the EPR thought
[L541] experiment to demonstrate that the Heisenberg uncer￾tainty principle fails if quantum mechanics is complete.
[L542] They first defined an "element of reality": If we can pre￾dict the value of a physical quantity without disturbing
[L543] the measured system, then that quantity is an element
[L544] of reality. In the EPR thought experiment, the state of
[L545] particle A is dependent on the state of particle B.
[L546] Let’s start with the momentum of particle B.
[L547] The momentum of particle A is measured and is found
[L548] to have a value of p. We can infer that the momentum
[L549] of particle B is equal in magnitude but opposite in direc￾tion, −p, due to the conservation of linear momentum.
[L550] This inference allows us to predict the value of particle
[L551] B’s momentum without actually measuring it.
[L552] Therefore, according to Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky,
[L553] the momentum of particle B is an element of reality.
[L554] Similarly, let’s consider the position of particle B.
[L555] We measure the position of particle A along the x￾axis and find it at position x1. According to the "con￾servation of relative position" (a principle invented by
[L556] Einstein), we can conclude that particle B’s position is
[L557] related to A’s position by a fixed separation, denoted as
[L558] x0. Specifically, particle B’s position can be expressed as
[L559] x2 = x1 + x0.
[L560] Again, without directly measuring the position of par￾ticle B, we can predict its value based on the measure￾ment of particle A. Thus, the position of particle B is
[L561] considered an element of reality.
[L562] This suggests that particle B’s momentum and posi￾tion can be simultaneously determined, contrary to the
[L563] uncertainty principle.
[L564] Indeed, Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky argued that
[L565] these elements of reality, namely the momentum and po￾sition of particle B, contradict the Heisenberg uncertainty
[L566] principle. The uncertainty principle states that momen￾tum and position cannot be precisely known simultane￾ously. The uncertainty principle represents the commu￾tation relationship between the operators for momentum
[L567] P and position Q, showing that they do not commute.
[L568] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky show that if quantum
[L569] mechanics is complete, momentum and position, with
[L570] two non-commuting operators P and Q, can have simul￾taneous reality.
[L571] According to Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky, since the
[L572] two particles no longer interact at the time of measure￾ment, no real change can occur in the second particle due
[L573] to anything that may be done to the first particle [1].
[L574] This is the principle of local realism: particles A and B
[L575] should only be influenced by their local interactions.
[L576] However, when particle A’s momentum is measured,
[L577] particle B’s momentum is inferred instantaneously with￾out disturbing particle A. This violates local realism.

[L579] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky thus conclude: quan￾tum mechanics is incomplete.

[L636] In this work, we explored a pathway to resolving these foundational tensions by proposing a novel
[L637] framework: direct-sum quantum field theory (DQFT). This construction stems from the longstanding
[L638] intuition, going back to Einstein and Rosen in 1935 [1], Schrödinger in 1956 [3], and ’t Hooft in recent
[L639] decades [21], that a consistent quantum gravitational description of nature must involve two sheets of
[L640] spacetime, or equivalently, two time directions connected through a quantum bridge.
[L641] The key insight of this paper is that gravitational horizons (in black holes, de Sitter, and Rindler
[L642] spacetimes) induce a natural partitioning of Hilbert space into geometric superselection sectors (SSS),
[L643] each defined by discrete spacetime symmetries such as parity (P) and time reversal (T ). These sectors
[L644] form a direct-sum structure, within which quantum fields remain globally unitary, even in spacetimes
[L645] where standard QFT predicts loss of information or thermality.
[L646] A unifying element in this picture is the inverted harmonic oscillator (IHO), whose quantum
[L647] properties were reviewed in Section 3, and which recurs across all horizon-based physics as a universal
[L648] effective degree of freedom. In Sec . 4 we showed that IHOs naturally encode the dynamics of quantum
[L649] fields near horizons, and for a successful description of quantum fields in curved spacetime, we
[L650] must necessarily understand our physical world with two arrows of time. In Sec. 5, we built the
[L651] direct-sum quantum field theory that gives a new understanding of spacetime based on discrete
[L652] transformations such as PT . This particular quantization structure with two arrows of time at the
[L653] parity conjugate regions gives a new geometrical understanding of IHO phase space envisioned
[L654] by Berry and Keating [22]. Our construction gives an understanding of quantum fields in curved
[L655] spacetime with direct-sum mathematical bridges that connect the sheets of spacetime related by
[L656] discrete space-time transformations. These mathematical bridges not only retain the vision of ER, but
[L657] also restore the unitarity in curved spacetime. According to this framework, a pure state is a direct-sum
[L658] (not a superposition) of two pure state components that represent the nature of the state within and
[L659] behind the horizon (See (137), (154), (165) and also (155)). The entanglement gets spread across the
[L660] gravitational horizon in the form of pure states dictated by discrete spacetime transformations. This
[L661] means that an observer not only witnesses pure states evolving into pure states but also can reconstruct
[L662] the information behind the horizon. The gravitational horizons in our construction act quantum
[L663] mechanically as "mirrors" so that we not only achieve unitarity but also observer complementarity.
[L664] This constitutes a first important step towards a consistent construction of QFTCS, which is essential
[L665] for building quantum gravity [11,18].
[L666] In Section 6, we reinterpreted the ER=EPR conjecture [48] through the lens of DQFT. Rather than
[L667] requiring geometric wormholes, we argue that entangled quantum states bridging PT -conjugate
[L668] regions realize mathematical Einstein-Rosen bridges within a single physical spacetime. This refor￾mulation not only preserves unitarity but naturally accommodates observer complementarity and
[L669] provides a field-theoretic underpinning to quantum connectivity across horizons. Historically, the
[L670] concept of a thermofield double state, introduced by Israel in 1976 [72], involved constructing a pure
[L671] quantum state in an enlarged Hilbert space that is a tensor product of two copies of the original space.
[L672] In this formalism, the second Hilbert space was considered fictitious, introduced merely to purify the

parts:
Got them. This is a useful set, and it separates pretty cleanly into three jobs for what we're doing.

First, the papers that bear directly on the ER filament construction. The original Einstein–Rosen paper remains the baseline. Katanaev’s *Passing the Einstein–Rosen Bridge* keeps the two-copy Schwarzschild construction explicit: the two exterior regions are glued at \(u=0\), corresponding to the horizon, and investigates smooth particle trajectories through that geometry. fileciteturn1file19L75-L90 The newer Gaztañaga/Kumar/Marto work is pursuing a rather different reinterpretation—two time directions/geometric sectors and horizon oscillator structure rather than an ordinary classical wormhole—so that may be useful particularly for the timesheet/time-direction side of H(s)H, but I would not let it overwrite the original ER geometry. fileciteturn1file14L18-L39

Second—and possibly immediately important given what you just said about charge—is Engelhardt, Freivogel & Iqbal, *Electric fields and quantum wormholes*. A classical ER bridge can carry electric flux through its throat. More interestingly, they explicitly separate

\[
\Phi_\Sigma=\Phi_R+\Phi_L
\]

from

\[
\Phi_\Delta=\frac{\Phi_R-\Phi_L}{2}.
\]

The first counts net enclosed charge and is quantized in charge units; the second measures electric field threading the wormhole and can vary continuously. fileciteturn2file4L261-L300

That distinction jumps out given the geometry you've just outlined. Standard physics itself is already separating:

\[
\boxed{\text{net charge}}
\]

from

\[
\boxed{\text{extended electric flux through the bridge}}.
\]

So we should absolutely examine whether your tentative division between intrinsic filament/bridge geometry and extended Kelvin-vortex/timesheet response has a counterpart there. I would not map them yet, but this paper gives us something concrete to map rather than an analogy. The authors explicitly invoke Wheeler's “charge without charge”: electric field lines threading nontrivial geometry without an ordinary localized charge source in the naive sense. fileciteturn2file0L25-L46

Third is the EPR/Bell constraint set: original EPR, Bell, Aspect, Clauser–Shimony, Freedman, Mermin, etc. These aren't likely to determine filament diameter, but they are an extremely hard constraint on what the finished worldtube geometry is allowed to do.

Bell's original result is particularly easy to state in our current language. You cannot have an underlying description in which the two outcomes are independently local functions

\[
A(\mathbf a,\lambda),\qquad B(\mathbf b,\lambda)
\]

of local analyzer settings and shared prior data \(\lambda\), and still reproduce all the quantum correlations. Bell explicitly identifies locality—one distant measurement result being unaffected by operations on the other system—as the crucial restriction. fileciteturn1file13L8-L27

That doesn't say a four-dimensional worldtube geometry is impossible. It tells us exactly what it must **not reduce to**: two locally self-contained particles carrying a classical instruction set away from a common source.

And that makes ER/EPR potentially relevant to our block-construction method for a very specific reason. If an entangled pair is represented as one globally constrained 4D geometrical object rather than two independent worldtubes plus hidden instructions, then Bell's factorization assumption is simply not the geometry being proposed. Whether that geometry reproduces the correlations is another calculation entirely—but at least we know where the tripwire is.

The historical ER/EPR papers you included are also useful here. Krizek emphasizes that Einstein's actual 1935 program was broader than the modern slogan: he hoped the many-bridge problem might eventually produce particle mass regularities and quantum restrictions from the bridge theory itself. fileciteturn2file2L131-L149 At the same time, that paper argues that the modern idea of using ER bridges specifically to explain EPR nonlocality should not simply be attributed back to Einstein. fileciteturn2file10L601-L625 That's a useful historical separation.

So for our immediate foundational work, I'd prioritize the uploaded material in this order:

1. **ER/Kerr/bridge geometry** → determine what the filament actually is and what transverse dimensions it inherits.
2. **Electric fields through ER bridges** → interrogate charge versus flux versus geometric distortion.
3. **EPR/Bell experiments** → constrain how multiple worldtubes can be globally related.
4. **Modern ER=EPR constructions** → inspect afterward for geometric mechanisms we've independently arrived at, rather than borrowing their theoretical machinery.

I also see that several of the Bell/Aspect/Fry files are duplicates, so we only need to treat each unique paper once.

The electric-flux paper is the one I'd open up next in detail. It seems unexpectedly close to the exact charge/bridge distinction you were just trying to resolve.

[L218] By examining this conjecture
[L219] in section VI, I ponder the possibility of Einstein’s con￾cepts, ER bridges, and the EPR paradox being inter￾twined unexpectedly.
[L220] II. EPR: ELEMENTS OF REALITY
[L221] In early March 1935, Einstein, Rosen, and Podol￾sky submitted the manuscript of the EPR paper, "Can
[L222] Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be
[L223] Considered Complete?", to Physical Review, and it was
[L224] published on May 15, 1935 [1]
[L225] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky used the EPR thought
[L226] experiment to demonstrate that the Heisenberg uncer￾tainty principle fails if quantum mechanics is complete.
[L227] They first defined an "element of reality": If we can pre￾dict the value of a physical quantity without disturbing
[L228] the measured system, then that quantity is an element
[L229] of reality. In the EPR thought experiment, the state of
[L230] particle A is dependent on the state of particle B.
[L231] Let’s start with the momentum of particle B.
[L232] The momentum of particle A is measured and is found
[L233] to have a value of p. We can infer that the momentum
[L234] of particle B is equal in magnitude but opposite in direc￾tion, −p, due to the conservation of linear momentum.
[L235] This inference allows us to predict the value of particle
[L236] B’s momentum without actually measuring it.
[L237] Therefore, according to Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky,
[L238] the momentum of particle B is an element of reality.
[L239] Similarly, let’s consider the position of particle B.
[L240] We measure the position of particle A along the x￾axis and find it at position x1. According to the "con￾servation of relative position" (a principle invented by
[L241] Einstein), we can conclude that particle B’s position is
[L242] related to A’s position by a fixed separation, denoted as
[L243] x0. Specifically, particle B’s position can be expressed as
[L244] x2 = x1 + x0.
[L245] Again, without directly measuring the position of par￾ticle B, we can predict its value based on the measure￾ment of particle A. Thus, the position of particle B is
[L246] considered an element of reality.
[L247] This suggests that particle B’s momentum and posi￾tion can be simultaneously determined, contrary to the
[L248] uncertainty principle.
[L249] Indeed, Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky argued that
[L250] these elements of reality, namely the momentum and po￾sition of particle B, contradict the Heisenberg uncertainty
[L251] principle. The uncertainty principle states that momen￾tum and position cannot be precisely known simultane￾ously. The uncertainty principle represents the commu￾tation relationship between the operators for momentum
[L252] P and position Q, showing that they do not commute.
[L253] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky show that if quantum
[L254] mechanics is complete, momentum and position, with
[L255] two non-commuting operators P and Q, can have simul￾taneous reality.
[L256] According to Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky, since the
[L257] two particles no longer interact at the time of measure￾ment, no real change can occur in the second particle due
[L258] to anything that may be done to the first particle [1].
[L259] This is the principle of local realism: particles A and B
[L260] should only be influenced by their local interactions.
[L261] However, when particle A’s momentum is measured,
[L262] particle B’s momentum is inferred instantaneously with￾out disturbing particle A. This violates local realism.
[L263] arXiv:2307.05548v2 [physics.hist-ph] 4 Sep 20232
[L264] Einstein, Rosen, and Podolsky thus conclude: quan￾tum mechanics is incomplete.

thoughts.content: I’m separating the bridge’s minimal throat from any speculative shell or helix. The supplied material supports an areal radius and bifurcation sphere, but it doesn’t yet establish a Kerr-specific cross-section or an emergent mass-based core scale.

I’m treating the core as the bridge’s minimal transverse geometry: a bifurcation sphere with areal radius \(r_h\), not a cylindrical tube, helical envelope, or particle-sized ring. Charge may thread it without uniquely fixing its radius.

parts:
Yes. If we strip everything else away, I think **the Core** should mean one very specific thing:

\[
\boxed{\text{the irreducible transverse geometry of the filament before it coils, braids, vibrates, or intersects a timesheet.}}
\]

On the papers we have, the cleanest candidate is the **minimal ER bridge section**.

For the ordinary Schwarzschild ER construction, the two exterior regions meet at the bifurcation sphere

\[
r=r_h,
\]

which in Einstein and Rosen's notation is \(r=2m\). Modern treatments likewise describe the \(t=0\) bridge as joining at that bifurcation \(S^2\). fileciteturn3file0L47-L58 fileciteturn3file1L90-L112

And \(r\) here is an **areal radius**:

\[
A_{\rm core}=4\pi r_h^2.
\]

So there is no ambiguity about what geometrical quantity the GR solution supplies. If we take a 3D slice through the filament, the primitive ER core is not a line and not really a cylindrical tube. It is a minimum-area spherical section connecting two continuations of the geometry.

There is an even better way to see its shape. On the time-symmetric Schwarzschild slice,

\[
d\ell^2=
\frac{dr^2}{1-r_h/r}+r^2d\Omega^2.
\]

Let \(\ell\) be proper distance measured away from the throat. Near \(r=r_h\),

\[
r(\ell)
=
r_h+\frac{\ell^2}{4r_h}+O(\ell^4).
\]

So locally it looks like

\[
\boxed{\text{minimum }S^2\ \longrightarrow\ \text{quadratic opening on either side}.}
\]

That's much more precise than “tube thickness.” The core has a minimum cross-section and immediately flares away from it.

For H(s)H, in the temporary block construction, I would therefore picture the filament not as

\[
\text{centerline}+\text{sheath},
\]

but as a continuous 4D structure whose local transverse sections contain this minimum bridge geometry. Coiling then deforms/organizes the **whole thing**. There is no separate object tracing a path.

Now, importantly, the charge papers tell us **not to identify the core scale with charge yet**. A classical ER bridge can have electric flux threaded through its throat, and Engelhardt et al. distinguish net charge,

\[
\Phi_\Sigma,
\]

from continuously adjustable field-through-the-bridge flux,

\[
\Phi_\Delta.
\]

Those are different quantities on the same bridge geometry. fileciteturn3file1L127-L149

That fits our present discipline nicely:

\[
\text{Core geometry}
\]

first;

then separately

\[
\text{what charge does to / through that geometry}.
\]

The original ER charged construction muddies the scale issue rather than settling it. Einstein and Rosen produced a separate charged, massless bridge solution, while treating charge and mass as independent constants; that's part of why they eventually regarded electron/proton as a multi-bridge problem. So I would not use that historical charged radius as *the* filament diameter without further reason. fileciteturn3file2L191-L203

The major unresolved piece is **rotation**.

If the actual particle filament is ER-like but spinning, then Schwarzschild's spherical minimum is probably only the zeroth-order case. We need to look at Kerr and especially Kerr–Newman spatial sections and ask:

\[
S^2\quad\longrightarrow\quad ?
\]

under angular momentum and charge.

Specifically we need to extract:

\[
\text{minimum transverse extent},
\]

\[
\text{major/minor radii if toroidal},
\]

\[
\text{ring parameter }a,
\]

\[
\text{horizon/ergosurface dimensions},
\]

and whether there is **any genuine finite excluded core**.

That last point matters for the Pauli idea. The standard Kerr *ring singularity itself* is a geometrical ring locus, not automatically a finite solid core. So if H(s)H needs an absolute nonintersection thickness, we cannot quietly equate “Kerr ring radius” with “hard filament diameter.” We need the 3D Kerr/ER geometry to tell us what region, if any, is actually irreducible.

So at this stage I would write the foundational decomposition as:

\[
\boxed{
\underbrace{\text{ER/Kerr minimum geometry}}_{\text{CORE}}
\;\rightarrow\;
\underbrace{\text{persistent winding}}_{\text{COIL}}
\;\rightarrow\;
\underbrace{\text{multiple wound cores}}_{\text{BRAID}}
}
\]

with timesheet distortion, Kelvin structure, charge, mass, etc. deliberately held out of the first box until we know what the bare core is.

And the current papers give us a solid Schwarzschild starting point:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Core}_{J=Q=0}
=
\text{minimal }S^2,\qquad
A=4\pi r_h^2.
}
\]

The Kerr papers should tell us what that becomes when \(J\neq0\). That is the next thing I would want before assigning a numerical filament diameter.

[L33] The concept of the irreducible mass (Mirr) has led to the mass-energy (M) formula of a Kerr￾Newman black hole (BH), in turn leading to an expression for its surface area S = 16πM2
[L34] irr. This
[L35] allowed as well the coeval identification of the reversible and irreversible transformations. The
[L36] concepts of extracted and extractable energy soon followed. This new conceptual framework avoids
[L37] inconsistencies recently evidenced in a repetitive Penrose process. We consider repetitive decays in
[L38] the ergosphere of an initially extreme Kerr BH and show that these processes are highly irreversible.
[L39] For each decay, including the BH capture of the particle falling into the horizon, the increase of
[L40] the irreducible mass is much larger than the extracted energy. Correspondingly, the horizon radius
[L41] increases. The energy extraction process saturates and stops when the horizon reaches the decay
[L42] radius. Thus, reaching a final non-rotating Schwarzschild BH state by this accretion process is
[L43] impossible. We have assessed such processes for three selected decay radii, r = 1.2M, 1.5M, and
[L44] 1.9M. The energy extracted until saturation is only 2.75%, 4.54%, and 2.45% of the BH initial
[L45] mass, while the extractable energy is reduced by 25%, 56%, and 92%. The BH rotational energy
[L46] is mostly converted into irreducible mass, which increases to 75%, 83%, and 95% of the initial BH
[L47] mass. Therefore, evaluating the effect of the irreducible mass increase in the energy extraction
[L48] processes in the Kerr BH ergosphere is now mandatory.

[L13] Abstract. Following the method of Hoenselaers and Perj´es we present a
[L14] new corrected and dimensionally consistent set of multipole gravitational and
[L15] electromagnetic moments for stationary axisymmetric spacetimes. Furthermore,
[L16] we use our results to compute the multipole moments, both gravitational and
[L17] electromagnetic, of a Kerr-Newman black hole.
[L18] 1. Introduction
[L19] After Ernst’s first paper on reformulating Einstein’s equations for stationary and
[L20] axisymmetric spacetimes (i) without [1], and (ii) with electromagnetic field [2],
[L21] Geroch and Hansen [3, 4] defined the multipole moments of static and stationary
[L22] spacetimes respectively, by measuring the deviation of the geometry from flatness in
[L23] the neighborhood of a point at infinity. Their definition of the moments is equivalent
[L24] to the one introduced by Thorne in [5]. Later, Simon and Beig [6] reconstructed the
[L25] moments from the series expansion of field variables, and Simon [7] generalized them so
[L26] as to include electrovacuum spacetimes. Especially the axisymmetric spacetimes that
[L27] Ernst studied are interesting physically, and can be fully described by a number of scalar
[L28] moments, in the same way that newtonian gravitational potentials are characterized by
[L29] their mass multipole moments.
[L30] In 1990 Hoenselaers and Perj´es [8] generalized the work of Fodor et al [9] on vacuum
[L31] gravitational moments to cases where spacetime is endowed with an electromagnetic
[L32] field that retains the axisymmetry of the metric. Although the generalization method
[L33] they used was right, an incorrect intermediate formula led to the contamination of
[L34] the final expressions for the moments with errors. In our paper we have tried to (i)
[L35] determine the root of these errors, (ii) give a few extra intermediate relations that are
[L36] used in the procedure of computing the moments, and (iii) correct the final expressions † e-mail:tsotiri@phys.uoa.gr ‡ e-mail:tapostol@cc.uoa.gr

[L3] Black hole candidates and the Kerr bound
[L4] Tomohiro Harada1(a) and Rohta Takahashi(b)
[L5] (a)Department of Physics, Rikkyo University, Toshima, Tokyo 175-8501, Japan
[L6] (b)Cosmic Radiation Laboratory, the Institute of Physical and Chemical Research, 2-1 Hirosawa, Wako,
[L7] Saitama 351-0198, Japan
[L8] Abstract
[L9] The specific angular momentum of a Kerr black hole must not be larger than its mass
[L10] in the geometrical units. The observational confirmation of this bound which we call
[L11] a Kerr bound directly suggests the existence of a black hole. On the other hand, the
[L12] violation of this bound may suggest the existence of a superspinning object which
[L13] might be suggested from a string theory argument. In order to investigate obser￾vational testability of this bound by using the X-ray energy spectrum of black hole
[L14] candidates, we calculate the energy spectra from an optically thick and geometrically
[L15] thin accretion disk of a superspinning object which is described by a Kerr metric
[L16] but whose specific angular momentum is larger than its mass, and then compare the
[L17] spectra of this object with those of a black hole. Based on this calculation, we present
[L18] that the observational confirmation of the Kerr bound is very hard but the violation
[L19] of it may be detectable if only the continuum X-ray spectrum of the disk is available.
[L20] 1 Introduction
[L21] Black hole candidates will be directly observed by radio interferometers by X-ray satellites and gravita￾tional wave detectors in the near future. Although these candidates are most likely to be black holes, it
[L22] is not obvious to confirm that. In principle, to prove that black hole candidates are really black holes, we
[L23] have to show that the observed data cannot be explained by anything else. In this relation, there is an
[L24] argument that if we can show that a sufficiently large amount of mass, say, above the model-independent
[L25] maximum mass of neutron stars ∼ 3M , is compactified within the size comparable with its gravitational
[L26] radius, general relativity assures that it is a black hole. It turns out however that this argument crucially
[L27] depends on the cosmic censorship hypothesis [1, 2]. The singularity theorems predict the existence of
[L28] spacetime singularities in generic spacetimes, where the spacetime curvature is singular in typical cases.
[L29] The cosmic censorship hypothesis is an unproven hypothesis about the properties of spacetimes which are
[L30] solutions to the Einstein equation with physically reasonable matter fields and with generic initial data.
[L31] It claims that spacetime singularities formed in physical gravitational collapse are covered by horizons
[L32] and hidden from any or distant observers. Thus, the cosmic censorship hypothesis ensures the future pre￾dictability of the classical theory including general relativity. On the other hand, since quantum gravity
[L33] should replace classical general relativity in the Planckian regime, singular spacetimes in classical theory
[L34] might be modified to regular ones in some sense. If this is true, the cosmic censorship hypothesis for the
[L35] classical theory should be reconsidered in the new context. One of the interesting possibilities is that
[L36] naked-singular solutions of the classical Einstein equation are physically significant in the low-curvature
[L37] region but largely modified to be smooth spacetimes around singularities in the classical solutions due
[L38] to quantum gravity effects. This article is based on Takahashi and Harada [3]. We use the geometrical
[L39] units, where c = G = 1.

[L4] This book gives a self-contained exposition of the theory of gravitational
[L5] solitons and provides a comprehensive review of exact soliton solutions to
[L6] Einstein’s equations.
[L7] The text begins with a detailed discussion of the extension of the inverse
[L8] scattering method to the theory of gravitation, starting with pure gravity and
[L9] then extending it to the coupling of gravity with the electromagnetic field. There
[L10] follows a systematic review of the gravitational soliton solutions based on their
[L11] symmetries. These solutions include some of the most interesting in gravita￾tional physics, such as those describing inhomogeneous cosmological models,
[L12] cylindrical waves, the collision of exact gravity waves, and the Schwarzschild
[L13] and Kerr black holes.
[L14] This work will equip the reader with the basic elements of the theory of
[L15] gravitational solitons as well as with a systematic collection of nontrivial
[L16] applications in different contexts of gravitational physics. It provides a valuable
[L17] reference for researchers and graduate students in the fields of general relativity,
[L18] string theory and cosmology, but will also be of interest to mathematical
[L19] physicists in general.

[L11] constrain the modes’ frequencies to 30% of the Kerr spectrum, providing a test of the remnant’s Kerr
[L12] nature. We also examine Hawking’s area law, also known as the second law of black hole mechanics, which
[L13] states that the total area of the black hole event horizons cannot decrease with time. A range of analyses that

[L19] measurement [4–6], have led the field from the first glimpse

[L21] hundreds of detections [9–18]. Here, we report the obser￾vation of GW250114_082203, henceforth GW250114,
[L22] shown in Fig. 1. With similar parameters to GW150914,
[L23] GW250114 reaches a similar strain amplitude of ∼10−21.
[L24] Yet, thanks to the LIGO detectors now operating near their
[L25] design sensitivity [3], it registers at a signal-to-noise ratio of
[L26] 80, as opposed to 26 for GW150914 a decade ago. This
[L27] makes GW250114 the most clearly recorded signal to date,
[L28] broadening the scope of fundamental tests of strong-field
[L29] gravity and black holes.
[L30] From a theoretical standpoint, black holes are expected
[L31] to be remarkably simple objects [22–30]. According to
[L32] Einstein’s theory of general relativity and under suitable
[L33] regularity assumptions, isolated stationary black holes
[L34] can be fully characterized by just three parameters: mass,
[L35] spin, and electromagnetic charge. For neutral black holes,
[L36] this implies that mass and spin determine the system
[L37] through the Kerr metric [31], the unique axisymmetric,
[L38] neutral solution to Einstein’s equations [26]. This unique￾ness is closely tied to key conjectures in classical
[L39] gravitation, including weak cosmic censorship [32] and
[L40] the stability of rotating black holes [33–39], both of
[L41] which remain unproven.
[L42] The uniqueness and implied featurelessness of black
[L43] holes gives rise to paradoxes in the context of quantum

[L54] interpretation of black hole entropy [44,51,52].

[L3] Mirjam Cvetič,
[L4] 1,2,* Nelson Hernández Rodríguez,3,† Maria J. Rodriguez,3,4,5,‡ and Oscar Varela 3,4,5,§

[L13] (Received 9 August 2024; accepted 2 June 2025; published 2 July 2025)
[L14] We derive the explicit embedding of the effective Kerr spacetimes, which are pertinent to the vanishing
[L15] of static Love numbers, soft hair descriptions of Kerr black holes, and low-frequency scalar-Kerr scattering
[L16] amplitudes, as solutions within N ¼ 2 supergravity. These spacetimes exhibit a hidden SLð2; RÞ × Uð1Þ or
[L17] SOð4; 2Þ symmetry resembling the so called subtracted geometries with SLð2; RÞ × SLð2; RÞ symmetry,
[L18] which accurately represent the near-horizon geometry of Kerr black holes and, as we will argue most
[L19] accurately represents the internal structure of the Kerr black hole. To quantify the differences among the
[L20] effective Kerr spacetimes, we compare their physical quantities, internal structures, and geodesic equations.
[L21] Although their thermodynamic properties, including entropy, match those of Kerr, our study uncovers
[L22] significant differences in the interiors of these effective Kerr solutions. A careful examination of the internal
[L23] structure of the spacetimes highlights the distinctions between various effective Kerr geometries and their
[L24] quasinormal spectra.
[L25] DOI: 10.1103/zp85-xym1
[L26] I. INTRODUCTION
[L27] Exploring low-frequency physics within black hole
[L28] backgrounds has proven highly fruitful for the soft hair
[L29] of Kerr black holes descriptions, low-frequency scalar-Kerr
[L30] scattering amplitudes and vanishing of the gravitational
[L31] static Love numbers for rotating black holes. The guiding
[L32] principle in this approach has been the observation that for
[L33] certain low frequency regimes, ω ≪ 1=M, with M the
[L34] black hole mass, one can explicitly realize a hidden
[L35] SLð2; RÞ × SLð2; RÞ symmetry in the massless Klein￾Gordon (KG) wave equation for a propagating field.
[L36] This symmetry does not manifest itself as an isometry of
[L37] the background metric.
[L38] One of the significant effective metrics associated with
[L39] Kerr black holes is the so-called subtracted geometry [1].
[L40] This is specifically connected to the hidden symmetries of
[L41] Kerr black hole spacetimes via Teukolsky’s equation in the
[L42] theory of gravitational perturbations as employed in [2].
[L43] The key feature is that these geometries provide an
[L44] approximation in the near-horizon region of a Kerr black
[L45] hole, maintaining its thermodynamic properties at the outer
[L46] event horizon and its internal structure.
[L47] An additional collection of fundamental geometries per￾tinent to black holes are the effective near-zone metrics that
[L48] play a crucial role in describing gravitational tidal deforma￾tions, or Love symmetries [3–5]. These different geometries
[L49] arise from the ambiguity in how one defines the effective
[L50] Kerr near zone expansion associated with a freedom to move
[L51] frequency dependent terms in the Klein-Gordon (KG)
[L52] equation. For each choice of near zone split, the leading
[L53] order massless wave equation enjoys a generalized local
[L54] hidden symmetry [6]. Two instances of Kerr effective
[L55] geometry (KEG) approximations have been recently pro￾posed. On the one hand, there is a geometry preserving an
[L56] SOð4; 2Þ found in [7] and, on the other hand, an effective
[L57] geometry preserving an SLð2; RÞ × Uð1Þ as shown in [8].
[L58] These are more mysterious than the SLð2; RÞ × SLð2; RÞ;
[L59] even-though these alternative KEGs preserve the same
[L60] thermodynamic properties of Kerr, they also realize distinct
[L61] hidden symmetries of the KG wave equation which could
[L62] explain the vanishing of the static Love numbers for Kerr
[L63] black holes. The KEG with SOð4; 2Þ or SLð2; RÞ × Uð1Þ

Yes. I’ll keep a running bibliography and only promote papers into it when they are actually doing work for the construction; duplicates, superseded versions, and merely pedagogical references won’t clutter it.

And this Kerr batch already sharpens “the Core” considerably.

The first thing to keep separate is that Kerr gives us at least three geometrically different candidate scales, not one:

\[
\boxed{a=\frac{J}{Mc}}
\]

the rotational length parameter;

\[
\boxed{r_+=M+\sqrt{M^2-a^2}}
\]

the Boyer–Lindquist outer-horizon coordinate in \(G=c=1\);

and the invariant horizon area

\[
\boxed{A_H=16\pi M_{\rm irr}^2}.
\]

The last one defines an invariant areal radius

\[
R_A\equiv\sqrt{\frac{A_H}{4\pi}}
=2M_{\rm irr}.
\]

For Kerr,

\[
M_{\rm irr}
=
\sqrt{\frac{Mr_+}{2}},
\]

so

\[
\boxed{R_A=\sqrt{2Mr_+}}.
\]

That distinction matters enormously for H(s)H: the **ring**, the **horizon coordinate radius**, and the **actual area scale of the horizon cross-section** are not interchangeable. Ruffini et al. explicitly give both the horizon relation and \(A_H=16\pi M_{\rm irr}^2\). fileciteturn5file10L629-L675

The classical Kerr singularity itself occurs at

\[
r=0,\qquad\theta=\frac{\pi}{2},
\]

i.e. a ring rather than the Schwarzschild point/spherical central singular structure. The horizon exists only when the Kerr bound is satisfied. fileciteturn5file1L63-L88

So at the moment I would **not** call the ring itself the finite core. It is a singular locus. The finite geometry surrounding it gives us better candidates for what H(s)H means operationally by filament cross-section.

But Carter's 1968 paper just became one of our most important sources.

Carter points out that \(a\) couples to mass to give angular momentum and to charge to give the asymptotic magnetic dipole moment \(ea\). Consequently the Kerr–Newman gyromagnetic ratio is \(e/m\), which he explicitly notes agrees with the simple Dirac electron result. Then he actually inserts electron-like parameters and remarks that the length scale determined by \(a\) is “about the same as the Compton radius.” fileciteturn5file6L379-L399

That is extremely relevant to the distinction we made earlier.

We had independently said:

\[
\text{filament dimension}\neq\text{coil dimension}.
\]

And now standard Kerr geometry itself supplies a rotational length

\[
a=\frac{J}{Mc}.
\]

For spin \(J=\hbar/2\),

\[
\boxed{
a=\frac{\hbar}{2mc}.
}
\]

That is exactly the half-reduced-Compton scale that appeared when we looked at the electron's ZB frequency,

\[
\omega_Z=\frac{2mc^2}{\hbar},
\qquad
a\,\omega_Z=c.
\]

But now we have to be much more careful about what that equality means. It may be telling us that **Kerr rotational geometry and the electron's persistent oscillatory geometry share a natural scale**, rather than that either one is straightforwardly “the filament diameter.”

And Carter found essentially this neighborhood of relations decades ago, including the Dirac-like gyromagnetic ratio. That paper is therefore mandatory.

There's another useful Kerr–Newman simplification. Sotiriou and Apostolatos find the complete gravitational and electromagnetic multipole sequences

\[
P_l=m(ia)^l,
\qquad
Q_l=e(ia)^l.
\]

So the electromagnetic multipoles have exactly the same geometric \(a\)-hierarchy as the gravitational multipoles, differing essentially by the overall \(e/m\) scaling. fileciteturn5file4L237-L249

Given your earlier thought that gravity and EM may be differently weighted manifestations of the same filament/timesheet/vortex geometry, that is a fact we definitely preserve. We don't interpret it yet; we put a marker beside it.

So I think our immediate “Core” anatomy is now:

\[
\boxed{\text{singular locus: Kerr ring}}
\]

inside

\[
\boxed{\text{rotation scale: }a=J/(Mc)}
\]

inside/associated with

\[
\boxed{\text{finite horizon cross-section: }A_H}
\]

with an external

\[
\boxed{\text{ergosphere / frame-dragged region}}
\]

and, for Kerr–Newman,

\[
\boxed{\text{EM and gravitational multipole structures sharing the same }a.}
\]

We should extract the actual 3D geometry of those nested surfaces next, especially their polar and equatorial dimensions. That will tell us whether the appropriate H(s)H “filament cross-section” looks like a disk/ring-centered structure, an oblate finite section, a throat section, or something that changes character depending on which slice we take.

Current running bibliography — **active sources only**:

1. Einstein & Rosen (1935), *The Particle Problem in the General Theory of Relativity*. Foundational bridge/particle construction.
2. Carter (1968), *Global Structure of the Kerr Family of Gravitational Fields*. **Core source** for Kerr/Kerr–Newman global geometry, ring structure, electron-scale \(a\), and gyromagnetic relation. fileciteturn4file7L2-L23
3. Sotiriou & Apostolatos (2004), *Corrections and Comments on the Multipole Moments of Axisymmetric Electrovacuum Spacetimes*. **Core source** for Kerr–Newman gravitational/EM multipole correspondence. fileciteturn4file2L13-L17
4. Engelhardt, Freivogel & Iqbal (2015), *Electric Fields and Quantum Wormholes*. **Core charge source** for charge versus flux through ER geometry. fileciteturn1file18L10-L17
5. Katanaev (2013), *Passing the Einstein–Rosen Bridge*. Useful for the original two-sheet geometry and throat crossing.
6. Ruffini et al. (2024), *The Role of the Irreducible Mass in Repetitive Penrose Energy Extraction Processes in a Kerr Black Hole*, using the later v4 as canonical. **Core dimensional source** for \(M_{\rm irr}\), horizon area, spin and horizon-radius relations. fileciteturn4file1L33-L50
7. Belinski & Verdaguer, *Gravitational Solitons*. Reference source for the solitonic/exact-solution side, potentially important when we get to the Kelvin/timesheet-bound-soliton question. fileciteturn4file6L3-L18

The duplicated \(2405.10459\) v1/v4 gets one bibliography entry, using v4. The two copies of arXiv:0407064v3 likewise get one entry.

The Carter result is the thing I would put a star beside right now. It connects the exact Kerr rotational scale, electron spin, magnetic moment structure, and the Compton neighborhood without our having asked it to. That is exactly the kind of externally constrained convergence we want.

Right. The bibliography should be selective, not archival.

I’ll keep three buckets mentally:

- core papers we actually rely on for the construction,
- secondary papers that materially constrain or clarify it,
- everything else we looked at but don’t need to cite or carry forward.

So, for example, Carter 1968 is clearly core. Einstein–Rosen 1935 is core. Engelhardt et al. may become core for the charge/flux question. Ruffini may or may not survive depending on whether we actually use irreducible mass/horizon area in the filament construction. The student notes and duplicate overview material probably won’t.

The running bibliography should reflect the argument we end up making, not the history of everything we opened.

The rotation parameter \(a\) is a length scale, not a literal diameter. The next step is choosing a spatial slice and calculating the corresponding equatorial, polar, and ring dimensions consistently.

[L112] The concept of the irreducible mass (Mirr) has led to the mass-energy (M) formula of a Kerr￾Newman black hole (BH), in turn leading to an expression for its surface area S = 16πM2
[L113] irr. This
[L114] allowed as well the coeval identification of the reversible and irreversible transformations. The
[L115] concepts of extracted and extractable energy soon followed. This new conceptual framework avoids
[L116] inconsistencies recently evidenced in a repetitive Penrose process. We consider repetitive decays in
[L117] the ergosphere of an initially extreme Kerr BH and show that these processes are highly irreversible.
[L118] For each decay, including the BH capture of the particle falling into the horizon, the increase of
[L119] the irreducible mass is much larger than the extracted energy. Correspondingly, the horizon radius
[L120] increases. The energy extraction process saturates and stops when the horizon reaches the decay
[L121] radius. Thus, reaching a final non-rotating Schwarzschild BH state by this accretion process is
[L122] impossible. We have assessed such processes for three selected decay radii, r = 1.2M, 1.5M, and
[L123] 1.9M. The energy extracted until saturation is only 2.75%, 4.54%, and 2.45% of the BH initial
[L124] mass, while the extractable energy is reduced by 25%, 56%, and 92%.

[L567] We studied the thermodynamical properties of a class of
[L568] KEGs on the black hole horizons. These geometries have
[L569] very different asymptotic structure compared to the asymp￾totically flat and asymptotically AdS case. The energy
[L570] density of such metrics typically falls off as inverse of the
[L571] radial distance and thus the geometry cannot have a finite
[L572] total energy. Within the KEG family, only for the SLð2; RÞ ×
[L573] SLð2; RÞ metric explicit expressions for the mass and
[L574] angular momentum are known [11]. For generic KEGs
[L575] the corresponding asymptotic charges, the mass and angular
[L576] momentum have not been explored in detail. New insights
[L577] there would clarify the first law of thermodynamics both at
[L578] the outer and inner horizon and that the Smarr formula holds.

[L598] Europe.
[L599] APPENDIX A: STU BLACK HOLES AND
[L600] SUBTRACTED GEOMETRIES
[L601] 1. Asymptotically flat black hole solution
[L602] Below is a summarized description of the general scaling
[L603] procedure for this type of effective Kerr solutions, as
[L604] described in [16,17]. For a detailed explanation, which
[L605] includes the reduction of the Kerr metric to 3 dimensions
[L606] MIRJAM CVETIČ et al. PHYS. REV. D 112, 026007 (2025)
[L607] 026007-10and its subsequent conversion back to 4 dimensions using
[L608] the Kaluza-Klein reduction rules, please refer to the
[L609] mentioned article.

At the moment, the cross-section is partly constrained but not yet uniquely fixed.

What we have with some confidence is this:

\[
\boxed{\text{filament core} \neq \text{coil diameter}}
\]

The coil comes later from persistent oscillation. The core has to come from the intrinsic ER/Kerr geometry itself.

For the nonrotating limit, Einstein–Rosen gives us a minimum spherical throat. In the Schwarzschild case the bridge joins at the minimum \(S^2\) surface, so the simplest transverse section is spherical in that limit.

Rotation changes that picture qualitatively. Kerr replaces the Schwarzschild central structure with a ring singularity at

\[
r=0,\qquad \theta=\frac{\pi}{2},
\]

and introduces the rotational length

\[
a=\frac{J}{Mc}.
\]

The uploaded Kerr material makes clear that the ring is literally an \(S^1\) locus in the equatorial plane, not a finite solid tube. fileciteturn5file8L540-L557 So \(a\) gives us the ring radius, but by itself it does **not** give us a finite filament thickness.

Around that ring we then have finite geometric surfaces: inner horizon, outer horizon, ergosurface, etc. The outer horizon is at

\[
r_+=M+\sqrt{M^2-a^2}
\]

for neutral Kerr. fileciteturn5file5L323-L337

But that \(r_+\) is a Boyer–Lindquist coordinate, not a literal Euclidean radius. The cleaner invariant measure is the horizon area,

\[
A_H=16\pi M_{\rm irr}^2,
\]

which gives an equivalent areal radius

\[
R_A=2M_{\rm irr}.
\]

That is a legitimate finite transverse scale. fileciteturn5file7L451-L459

So right now the core looks schematically like:

\[
\boxed{
\text{ring seed }(a)
\subset
\text{finite Kerr throat/horizon geometry}
\subset
\text{ergospheric distortion}
}
\]

rather than simply a round wire.

And for an electron specifically, the really interesting constraint is that

\[
a=\frac{J}{Mc}
\]

with

\[
J=\frac{\hbar}{2}
\]

gives

\[
\boxed{
a_e=\frac{\hbar}{2m_ec}.
}
\]

Carter explicitly noted that the Kerr \(a\)-scale for electron-like parameters lies around the Compton scale and that Kerr–Newman has the Dirac electron gyromagnetic ratio. fileciteturn5file6L356-L375

But that still tells us the **ring radius**, not the thickness of the finite excluded core.

So the unresolved geometric question is now very precise:

> On a suitable 3D spatial slice through Kerr/Kerr–Newman, what finite region naturally surrounds the ring, and what are its equatorial and polar dimensions?

That is what we need to calculate next.

My current best sketch would be something like this in transverse section:

```text
               polar direction
                    │
              _____ │ _____
           .-'      │      '-.
         .'         │         '.
        /      finite Kerr       \
       |      horizon/throat      |
       |                           |
       |      ○─────────○          | ← ring locus / a-scale
        \                         /
         '.                     .'
           '-._______________.-'
                    │
                 equator
```

But even that drawing is too spherical for rapidly rotating Kerr. The actual section should become increasingly oblate as \(a/M\) increases, while the ring sits in the equatorial plane.

So in terms of the quantities we eventually want for H(s)H, we currently have:

\[
\boxed{R_{\rm ring}=a}
\]

known from \(J/M\);

\[
\boxed{A_{\rm core}\ \text{or}\ R_A}
\]

available from horizon geometry;

but

\[
\boxed{d_{\rm polar}},\qquad
\boxed{d_{\rm equatorial}}
\]

still need to be worked out from the intrinsic horizon/throat metric rather than guessed.

Once we have those, we can finally ask whether the cross-section is approximately circular, oblate, toroidal/ring-centered, or something more subtle—and only then compare that intrinsic core size to the electron coil radius.

That is where we are.

metadata.reasoning_title: Analyzing electron Kerr geometry and size constraints

parts:
Yes. There is quite a lot we can leverage, but we should separate quantities that genuinely constrain the intrinsic cross-section from ones that constrain the later coil.

The first major point is that for an electron, the classical Kerr/Kerr–Newman black-hole horizon is not available as a literal core boundary. With electron parameters,

\[
a=\frac{J}{mc}\approx \frac{\hbar}{2m_ec}\sim 1.93\times 10^{-13}\ {\rm m},
\]

while its gravitational mass length

\[
M_g=\frac{Gm_e}{c^2}
\]

is about \(10^{-57}\) m. So the electron is fantastically over-extreme in classical Kerr–Newman terms: \(a\gg M_g\), and the usual horizon condition fails. Carter was already working in essentially this parameter regime when he noted that the Kerr \(a\)-scale for electron-like parameters is around the Compton scale. fileciteturn5file6L356-L375

That means the quantities worth mining are not “electron horizon radius,” but observables that constrain the geometry around the Kerr ring.

The strongest empirical handles are probably these:

- **Mass \(m\)** and **spin \(J=\hbar/2\)** give \(a=J/(mc)\) exactly within the proposed Kerr mapping. This fixes the ring/rotational scale, not thickness.
- **Magnetic moment and \(g\)-factor** constrain how charge is distributed relative to that rotation. CODATA gives
  \[
  g_e=-2.00231930436092(36),
  \]
  versus the ideal Kerr–Newman/Dirac value \(g=2\). The fractional anomaly is
  \[
  a_e=1.15965218046(18)\times10^{-3}.
  \]
  citeturn937958search44turn937958search2
- **Electric dipole moment limits** constrain any persistent fore–aft or parity-breaking distortion of the electron cross-section. That could be especially useful for deciding whether an admissible core is axisymmetric, slightly displaced, or intrinsically chiral.
- **High-energy scattering limits on electron spatial structure** are a brutal constraint. LEP analyses have put effective electron-size limits at roughly
  \[
  r_e \lesssim 10^{-19}\ {\rm m}
  \]
  in contact-interaction interpretations; one combined LEP analysis quotes \(1.1\times10^{-19}\) m. citeturn586091search50

That last number is important because it is about six orders of magnitude smaller than

\[
a_e\sim 10^{-13}\ {\rm m}.
\]

So if \(a\) is part of the H(s)H electron geometry, it cannot simply behave experimentally like an ordinary rigid charged body of radius \(a\). The geometry has to explain why scattering sees the electron as pointlike down to \(\sim10^{-19}\) m while the intrinsic rotational/phase scale is \(\sim10^{-13}\) m.

That distinction may actually help us separate **core** from **coil**:

\[
\boxed{\text{ordinary scattering size}\lesssim10^{-19}\ {\rm m}}
\]

versus

\[
\boxed{\text{Kerr/ZB rotational scale}\sim10^{-13}\ {\rm m}}.
\]

That is exactly the kind of six-order-of-magnitude separation one would expect if the latter is winding amplitude or 4D structure rather than literal material thickness.

For composite particles we have much richer direct spatial information. CODATA 2022 gives the proton rms charge radius

\[
r_p=0.84075(64)\ {\rm fm},
\]

and also extremely precise proton mass and magnetic moment data. citeturn586091search49turn937958search6 The neutron gives a measured mean-square charge radius

\[
\langle r_n^2\rangle=-0.1155(17)\ {\rm fm^2},
\]

which tells us about the signed radial charge structure even though the net charge is zero. citeturn586091search48

Those are excellent for the later braid construction because we can compare:

\[
\text{mass},\quad
J,\quad
\mu,\quad
r_{\rm charge},\quad
G_E(Q^2),\quad
G_M(Q^2).
\]

The full electromagnetic form factors are much more valuable than a single radius. If we construct a candidate cross-section/braid and calculate its form factor, the data tell us whether the geometry is remotely viable across momentum transfer rather than merely at \(Q^2\to0\).

For nuclei, the same thing gets even better: \(^3\)He and tritium form factors, charge radii, magnetic moments, spin, binding energies, etc. There are public electron-scattering datasets going back decades; \(^3\)He charge form factors have been measured over substantial momentum-transfer ranges. citeturn586091search6

So I think the empirical attack on the core should proceed in this order:

1. **Electron:** use \(m,J,\mu,g\), EDM limits, and pointlike-scattering limits. This tells us how large an intrinsic Kerr-like structure may be without acting like an ordinary extended charged object.
2. **Muon:** repeat the same construction. Because \(a\propto1/m\), the rotational scale changes by the known mass ratio while charge and spin remain the same. CODATA gives the reduced muon Compton wavelength \(1.867594306(42)\times10^{-15}\) m. citeturn937958search1 This is an unusually clean minimal-pair test.
3. **Proton/neutron:** use measured form factors and radii to constrain the first composite/braided cross-section.
4. **\(^3\)He/tritium:** constrain the next nesting level.

For the actual finite filament thickness, though, the electron scattering limit may currently be our most useful direct empirical ceiling:

\[
\boxed{d_{\rm core}\ll a_e}
\]

and plausibly

\[
\boxed{d_{\rm core}\lesssim 10^{-19}\ {\rm m}}
\]

if the core couples to scattering in anything like an ordinary spatially extended electron.

That is not yet an equality. It is a constraint.

The other route is theoretical rather than empirical: look for a regularized Kerr/ER geometry that supplies a finite thickness around the ring. Then the experiment tells us whether that proposed thickness survives.

If you want to dig data, the most valuable public archive haul would be raw or tabulated **electron/muon scattering limits, proton \(G_E/G_M\), neutron \(G_E/G_M\), and \(^3\)He/tritium elastic form factors**. CODATA/PDG can anchor the scalar constants; the scattering databases give us the shape information.

thoughts.content: I’m prioritizing downloadable differential cross sections with uncertainties and correlations: LEP large-angle Bhabha scattering, LEP muon-pair production, and compositeness searches. For hadrons, I’m treating proton/neutron form-factor datasets as a separate follow-up.

I’m targeting LEP-II HEPData records from 183–209 GeV: Bhabha, muon-pair, and tau-pair differential cross sections, covariance information, and Standard Model predictions. I’m giving highest priority to high-momentum-transfer angular distributions.

parts:
For the **core-cross-section problem**, I want data that tell us how far we can depart from an exactly pointlike electron or muon before high-\(Q^2\) scattering notices. I’d rather fit the data ourselves than inherit somebody else’s “electron radius,” because those published radius limits are model-dependent.

The main place to mine is **HEPData**. CERN Open Data is much less useful for this particular job; HEPData has the numerical LEP tables already unfolded into cross sections.

What I want first, in priority order:

1. **LEP2 large-angle Bhabha scattering, \(e^+e^-\to e^+e^-\).** This is the single most useful dataset for the electron core. Search HEPData for:
   - `"non-radiative E+ E- --> E+ E-" 189 207 GeV`
   - `"Bhabha" LEP2 differential cross section`
   - DELPHI, OPAL, L3, ALEPH separately.

   DELPHI has differential tables at 189, 192, 196, 200, 202, 205 and 207 GeV. citeturn440094search2 OPAL likewise has high-energy electron-pair angular distributions and uses the same data for contact-interaction limits. citeturn440094search7

   **Download the actual tables**, preferably YAML or CSV, including:
   \[
   \sqrt s,\quad \cos\theta\ {\rm bins},\quad
   \frac{d\sigma}{d\cos\theta},
   \]
   statistical errors, systematic errors, and any covariance/correlation matrices. If the SM prediction is included as a separate column/table, grab that too.

2. **The matching muon and tau channels from the same experiments and energies:**
   \[
   e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-,
   \qquad
   e^+e^-\to\tau^+\tau^-.
   \]
   This is important because electron–muon–tau are our clean minimal-pair/triple system: same charge and spin, vastly different mass. DELPHI has non-radiative \(\mu^+\mu^-\) differential distributions from 183 through 207 GeV. citeturn440094search1 OPAL has corresponding electron, muon and tau angular distributions in the same submission. citeturn440094search6

   If we can compare all three with the same detector/analysis conventions, that's ideal.

3. **L3 high-\(Q^2\) Bhabha / running-\(\alpha\) data.** Search:
   - `"Measurement of the Running of the Electromagnetic Coupling at Large Momentum-Transfer at LEP"`
   - L3, 189–209 GeV.

   They used about 40,000 Bhabha events and covered
   \[
   1800<-Q^2<21600\ {\rm GeV}^2,
   \]
   so this gives us an especially clean lever arm in momentum transfer. citeturn320573search9 If HEPData has the \(Q^2\)-binned differential tables, grab everything.

4. From **CERN Document Server**, grab this specific paper if you don't already have it:
   **D. Bourilkov, “Search for TeV Strings and New Phenomena in Bhabha Scattering at CERN LEP2,” Phys. Rev. D 62, 076005 (2000), hep-ph/0002172.**
   
   It combined ALEPH/L3/OPAL Bhabha data and explicitly fitted a fermion form factor
   \[
   F(Q^2)=1+\frac16Q^2r^2
   \]
   to obtain
   \[
   r_e<2.8\times10^{-19}\ {\rm m}
   \]
   at 95% CL. citeturn320573search43turn320573search0 I want this mostly as a **calibration check**: if our independent fit to the raw LEP data reproduces their scale, we know our machinery is sane.

What I **do not** especially need yet are generic compositeness searches, excited-electron mass limits, or exotic-model bounds unless they contain useful raw angular distributions. Those turn the data into somebody else's model too early.

The key mathematical object we're trying to recover from these tables is something like

\[
F(Q^2)
=
1+\frac16\langle r^2\rangle Q^2
+c_4Q^4+\cdots,
\]

without assuming at first that \(F\) describes a literal spherical charge ball. The \(Q^2\) dependence gives us a transverse scale; the angular dependence may eventually tell us whether an anisotropic/ring-like cross-section is allowed.

So if you're sitting in HEPData now, the **best first haul** would be:

**DELPHI + OPAL LEP2 \(e,e;\mu,\mu;\tau,\tau\) differential angular distributions, with all errors and correlations.**

If it's convenient, just download the complete HEPData submission archives rather than picking tables individually. Give me those ZIP/YAML files and I can sort out what we actually need.

After that, I’ll point you toward the proton/neutron/\(^3\)He form-factor archives—but those are a second stage.

parts:
Yes — you’re in the right general ecosystem, but **HepMC is not the database I meant**. HepMC is an event-record format/library used to represent Monte Carlo particle events. Useful later, but not where I’d start for this cross-section question.

From the CERN Open Data page you have open, I’d pivot specifically into **DELPHI**, because CERN has now released both actual LEP collision data and matching simulation samples there. That is better than I initially implied: we may be able to work much closer to event level rather than relying only on published summary tables.

For example, CERN Open Data has real DELPHI collision datasets from LEP2 at 181–210 GeV. One 1999 sample, `alld99_e196_e1`, contains about 4.36 million events in XShort DST form; there are 2000 datasets with millions more. citeturn150907search2turn150907search0 There are also dedicated Bhabha simulations at the same energies, including barrel and forward samples. One barrel Bhabha sample at ~188 GeV is only about 88 MB, while some high-statistics forward samples run into several GB. citeturn252670search0turn252670search1

So from where you are now, I’d search/filter for:

`DELPHI` → `181-210 GeV` → `e+e-`

and distinguish **Collision** from **Simulated**.

What I want first is not 70 GB of everything. I want a small, tractable matched pair:

- a real LEP2 DELPHI XShortDST collision sample near 189–207 GeV;
- its Bhabha \(e^+e^-\to e^+e^-\) simulation sample, preferably barrel first.

That lets us establish the analysis machinery before deciding whether it is worth hauling millions of events.

And yes, there are Gits we can leverage. CERN's DELPHI “Getting started” documentation points to actual DELPHI source and examples on CERN GitLab. The analysis framework is `dstana`/`skelana`; there is an examples repository and a newer `modern-delphi-examples` repository intended to show how to access the data from things like C++. The stack is also available in Docker, so in principle we can reconstruct the original analysis environment rather than reverse-engineering XShortDST ourselves. citeturn550381search0

The relevant source locations are linked from CERN's guide:

urlDELPHI getting-started guidehttps://opendata.cern.ch/docs/delphi-getting-started

and CERN says the source tree is under `gitlab.cern.ch/delphi`, with example repositories there; some modules still require CERN authentication, but the open examples should tell us how much we can do unauthenticated. citeturn550381search0

There's also a GitHub repository containing the source metadata/content behind CERN Open Data itself. That may be useful for programmatically locating datasets rather than clicking through thousands of records. citeturn252670search12

So I’d slightly revise our plan:

**Don't download a mountain of data yet.** Open DELPHI in the portal and find one high-energy real collision record plus one Bhabha simulation record. Send me the links—or just tell me what records you see—and I’ll tell you exactly which files from each are worth pulling.

Once we have the analysis pipeline working, we can decide whether to use the full event-level data or whether HEPData's already-corrected differential cross sections are the smarter source for the precision constraint. DELPHI itself cautions that reproducing old high-precision analyses from raw data is difficult because detector/run knowledge has been lost, which is a good reason to use the raw releases for geometry exploration and published HEPData numbers for the quantitative bound. citeturn252670search36

from pathlib import Path

script = r'''#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
cern_raw.py — thin, conservative wrapper around CERN's official
cernopendata-client for inspecting and acquiring CERN Open Data files.

Why a wrapper?
- Keeps us from accidentally downloading an entire multi-GB/TB record.
- Makes manifests before downloads.
- Supports HTTP/HTTPS and XRootD locations.
- Uses CERN's client for file-index expansion, checksum metadata, and downloads.

Dependency:
    python -m pip install -U cernopendata-client

Examples:
    # Inspect a DELPHI record by DOI:
    python cern_raw.py files --doi 10.7483/OPENDATA.DELPHI.JUHY.E2AF

    # Or try a record identifier:
    python cern_raw.py files --recid delphi-87218

    # Write an XRootD manifest without downloading:
    python cern_raw.py manifest --doi 10.7483/OPENDATA.DELPHI.JUHY.E2AF \
        --protocol xrootd -o delphi_87218_manifest.json

    # Dry-run the first file only:
    python cern_raw.py download --doi 10.7483/OPENDATA.DELPHI.JUHY.E2AF \
        --range 1-1

    # Actually download + verify first file:
    python cern_raw.py download --doi 10.7483/OPENDATA.DELPHI.JUHY.E2AF \
        --range 1-1 --yes --verify

    # Print XRootD endpoints for remote streaming:
    python cern_raw.py stream --doi 10.7483/OPENDATA.DELPHI.JUHY.E2AF
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Optional

CLIENT = "cernopendata-client"
SERVER = "https://opendata.cern.ch"


@dataclass
class FileEntry:
    index: int
    url: str
    size_bytes: Optional[int] = None
    checksum: Optional[str] = None

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return self.url.rstrip("/").rsplit("/", 1)[-1]


def die(msg: str, code: int = 2) -> None:
    print(f"ERROR: {msg}", file=sys.stderr)
    raise SystemExit(code)


def require_client() -> None:
    if shutil.which(CLIENT) is None:
        die(
            "cernopendata-client was not found.\n"
            "Install it with:\n"
            "  python -m pip install -U cernopendata-client"
        )


def selector_args(args: argparse.Namespace) -> list[str]:
    supplied = [
        ("--recid", getattr(args, "recid", None)),
        ("--doi", getattr(args, "doi", None)),
        ("--title", getattr(args, "title", None)),
    ]
    selected = [(flag, val) for flag, val in supplied if val]
    if len(selected) != 1:
        die("Supply exactly one of --recid, --doi, or --title.")
    flag, val = selected[0]
    return [flag, str(val)]


def run_client(cmd: list[str], capture: bool = False) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    require_client()
    full = [CLIENT, *cmd]
    return subprocess.run(
        full,
        text=True,
        capture_output=capture,
        check=False,
    )


def parse_verbose_file_list(text: str) -> list[FileEntry]:
    """
    Expected CERN client verbose lines are roughly:
      URL    SIZE    adler32:CHECKSUM

    We intentionally parse leniently so plain URL-only lines still work.
    """
    entries: list[FileEntry] = []
    for raw in text.splitlines():
        line = raw.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith(("==>", "NOTE", "WARNING", "ERROR")):
            continue

        # Find URL first; tolerate informational prefixes.
        m = re.search(r'((?:https?|root)://\S+)', line)
        if not m:
            continue
        url = m.group(1)
        rest = line[m.end():].strip()

        size = None
        checksum = None

        # First integer after URL is normally bytes.
        sm = re.search(r'\b(\d+)\b', rest)
        if sm:
            try:
                size = int(sm.group(1))
            except ValueError:
                pass

        cm = re.search(r'\b(?:adler32|md5|sha1|sha256):[0-9A-Fa-f]+\b', rest)
        if cm:
            checksum = cm.group(0)

        entries.append(FileEntry(len(entries) + 1, url, size, checksum))
    return entries


def get_files(args: argparse.Namespace, protocol: Optional[str] = None) -> list[FileEntry]:
    protocol = protocol or args.protocol
    cmd = [
        "get-file-locations",
        *selector_args(args),
        "--server", SERVER,
        "--protocol", protocol,
        "--verbose",
    ]
    if getattr(args, "no_expand", False):
        cmd.append("--no-expand")
    else:
        cmd.append("--expand")

    proc = run_client(cmd, capture=True)
    if proc.returncode != 0:
        sys.stderr.write(proc.stderr)
        die("CERN client could not retrieve file locations.", proc.returncode)

    files = parse_verbose_file_list(proc.stdout)
    if not files:
        # Some versions may put useful output on stderr or format differently.
        print(proc.stdout)
        if proc.stderr:
            print(proc.stderr, file=sys.stderr)
        die("No file URLs could be parsed from the client output.")
    return files


def human_bytes(n: Optional[int]) -> str:
    if n is None:
        return "?"
    x = float(n)
    units = ["B", "KiB", "MiB", "GiB", "TiB"]
    for u in units:
        if x < 1024 or u == units[-1]:
            return f"{x:.2f} {u}" if u != "B" else f"{int(x)} B"
        x /= 1024
    return f"{n} B"


def print_file_table(files: list[FileEntry]) -> None:
    print(f"{'#':>4}  {'size':>12}  {'checksum':<22}  file")
    print("-" * 100)
    for f in files:
        print(
            f"{f.index:>4}  {human_bytes(f.size_bytes):>12}  "
            f"{(f.checksum or '-'):22}  {f.name}"
        )
    known = [f.size_bytes for f in files if f.size_bytes is not None]
    if known:
        print("-" * 100)
        print(f"{len(files)} files; known total = {human_bytes(sum(known))}")
    else:
        print(f"{len(files)} files")


def cmd_metadata(args: argparse.Namespace) -> None:
    proc = run_client([
        "get-metadata",
        *selector_args(args),
        "--server", SERVER,
    ])
    raise SystemExit(proc.returncode)


def cmd_files(args: argparse.Namespace) -> None:
    print_file_table(get_files(args))


def cmd_manifest(args: argparse.Namespace) -> None:
    files = get_files(args)
    manifest = {
        "server": SERVER,
        "selector": {
            "recid": args.recid,
            "doi": args.doi,
            "title": args.title,
        },
        "protocol": args.protocol,
        "expanded_indexes": not args.no_expand,
        "files": [asdict(f) | {"name": f.name} for f in files],
    }
    out = Path(args.output)
    out.write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"Wrote {out} with {len(files)} file entries.")


def cmd_stream(args: argparse.Namespace) -> None:
    # XRootD endpoints only; no download.
    args.protocol = "xrootd"
    files = get_files(args, protocol="xrootd")
    chosen = files
    if args.range:
        chosen = select_range(files, args.range)
    for f in chosen:
        print(f.url)


def select_range(files: list[FileEntry], spec: str) -> list[FileEntry]:
    """
    Parse CERN-style ranges: 1-3,7,10-12
    """
    wanted: set[int] = set()
    for token in spec.split(","):
        token = token.strip()
        if not token:
            continue
        if "-" in token:
            a, b = token.split("-", 1)
            lo, hi = int(a), int(b)
            if lo > hi:
                lo, hi = hi, lo
            wanted.update(range(lo, hi + 1))
        else:
            wanted.add(int(token))
    return [f for f in files if f.index in wanted]


def cmd_download(args: argparse.Namespace) -> None:
    # Show what the record contains before doing anything.
    files = get_files(args)
    print_file_table(files)

    cmd = [
        "download-files",
        *selector_args(args),
        "--server", SERVER,
        "--protocol", args.protocol,
    ]

    if args.regexp:
        cmd += ["--filter-regexp", args.regexp]
    if args.name:
        cmd += ["--filter-name", args.name]
    if args.range:
        cmd += ["--filter-range", args.range]
    if args.verify:
        cmd.append("--verify")

    if args.protocol == "xrootd":
        cmd += ["--download-engine", "xrootd"]
    elif args.engine:
        cmd += ["--download-engine", args.engine]

    # Safety default: dry run.
    if not args.yes:
        cmd.append("--dry-run")
        print("\nDRY RUN ONLY. Re-run with --yes to download.\n")
    else:
        print("\nStarting download...\n")

    proc = run_client(cmd)
    raise SystemExit(proc.returncode)


def add_selector(p: argparse.ArgumentParser) -> None:
    g = p.add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)
    g.add_argument("--recid", help="CERN Open Data record ID")
    g.add_argument("--doi", help="Record DOI")
    g.add_argument("--title", help="Exact record title")


def add_file_options(p: argparse.ArgumentParser) -> None:
    p.add_argument(
        "--protocol",
        choices=["http", "xrootd"],
        default="http",
        help="Location/download protocol (default: http)",
    )
    p.add_argument(
        "--no-expand",
        action="store_true",
        help="Do not expand file-index records.",
    )


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Safe CERN Open Data record/file access wrapper."
    )
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    q = sub.add_parser("metadata", help="Show record metadata.")
    add_selector(q)
    q.set_defaults(func=cmd_metadata)

    q = sub.add_parser("files", help="List files, sizes, and checksums.")
    add_selector(q)
    add_file_options(q)
    q.set_defaults(func=cmd_files)

    q = sub.add_parser("manifest", help="Write a JSON manifest; no download.")
    add_selector(q)
    add_file_options(q)
    q.add_argument("-o", "--output", default="cern_manifest.json")
    q.set_defaults(func=cmd_manifest)

    q = sub.add_parser("stream", help="Print XRootD URLs; no download.")
    add_selector(q)
    q.add_argument("--range", help="Optional file range, e.g. 1-2,5")
    q.add_argument("--no-expand", action="store_true")
    q.set_defaults(protocol="xrootd", func=cmd_stream)

    q = sub.add_parser("download", help="Dry-run or download selected files.")
    add_selector(q)
    add_file_options(q)
    q.add_argument("--range", help="CERN-style file range, e.g. 1-2,5-7")
    q.add_argument("--name", help="Exact file name filter.")
    q.add_argument("--regexp", help="Regular-expression file-name filter.")
    q.add_argument(
        "--engine",
        choices=["requests", "pycurl"],
        default="pycurl",
        help="HTTP download engine; pycurl supports resume in CERN's Python client.",
    )
    q.add_argument("--verify", action="store_true", help="Verify after download.")
    q.add_argument(
        "--yes",
        action="store_true",
        help="Actually download. Without this flag, download is a dry run.",
    )
    q.set_defaults(func=cmd_download)

    return p


def main() -> None:
    parser = build_parser()
    args = parser.parse_args()
    args.func(args)
